messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 22
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Accountant
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 34

At 22, she is one of the youngest people in the accounting office where she works, known for keeping her spreadsheets immaculate and catching errors others miss. She is quiet, reliable, and quick with numbers, but the steadiness she shows at work feels hard won. When she talks about what happened, she begins not with herself but with her son, and with the week she is sure she aged years.

Her son is still a toddler when he becomes suddenly ill. At first she tells herself it is a fever, something common, something that will pass with rest and fluids. She is a young single mother, used to stretching money, time, and energy, used to making practical decisions under pressure. But over the course of a day his breathing changes and his body becomes frighteningly limp in her arms. She remembers the way his skin feels too hot and then strangely cool, the sound of herself calling his name too loudly, as if volume alone could pull him back toward her. In the emergency department, everything moves fast and not fast enough. Staff rush around him, using words she does not fully understand, and she stands there feeling useless, watching other people touch her child while she can do nothing except pray and answer questions.

The hours in the hospital blur together under harsh lights. Machines beep; shoes squeak down the hallway; someone keeps opening and closing a curtain. She sits upright in a plastic chair and cannot rest. Every time his monitor shifts or a nurse enters the room, her chest tightens. She is certain, again and again, that he is about to die. She bargains silently with God. She rehearses what she should have noticed sooner, what she should have done differently, even while doctors tell her she brought him in when she needed to. She cannot absorb their reassurance. What stays with her is the image of his small body in the hospital bed, connected to wires, and the unbearable thought that she might have to leave the hospital without him.

He survives, and others expect that relief will close the story. Instead, she says, that is when something in her begins to stay on alert all the time. Once he is discharged, she brings him home and tries to return to normal life, but home no longer feels safe in the same easy way. She checks his breathing repeatedly while he sleeps, sometimes holding her own breath until she sees his chest rise. If he naps longer than usual, panic surges through her before she can talk herself down. A mild cough, a warm forehead, even unusual quiet can send her back into the hospital room in her mind. She keeps his medications, discharge papers, and thermometer arranged with accountant-like precision, as if perfect organization might protect him.

At work, the habits that make her good at accounting become entangled with fear. She reviews invoices three and four times because her concentration slips whenever a memory intrudes. The sound of a medical drama playing on a coworker’s phone in the break room makes her hands go cold. If her daycare calls, even for something minor, her stomach drops instantly and she struggles to hear the rest of the message. She tries to hide this. She tells colleagues she is tired, that her son kept her up, and then returns to her desk and stares at columns of numbers that suddenly seem to swim on the screen.

Sleep becomes one of the clearest ways the experience continues to live in her. She falls asleep late because she checks on her son over and over, then wakes from dreams in which she is back in the emergency department, unable to reach him. Some nights she wakes already sitting up, heart pounding, listening for him. In the morning she feels ashamed of how exhausted and irritable she is. She snaps at family members who tell her she worries too much. When her mother offers to babysit, she wants the help but also feels a rush of dread at being separated from him. She texts constantly for updates, asking whether he has eaten, whether he seems warm, whether he is acting normal.

She does not think of herself as fragile. She gets up, goes to work, pays bills, and takes care of her child. But she lives as if disaster is always one room away. She avoids driving past the hospital unless she has to. She keeps busy because quiet moments leave too much space for images she does not want. At times she feels detached from friends her age, especially when they talk about dating, parties, or future plans. Her life feels divided into before her son got sick and after. In session, she speaks with composure until she reaches the part where she thought he might die, and then her voice thins. What troubles her most is not only the memory of that week, but the way her body still seems to believe it is happening.
